findings.evidence: `public_vh` removes the three identity headers before routing (`request_headers_to_remove: x-fleet-user, x-fleet-roles, x-fleet-tenant`, lines 63-66) with the comment 'Identity is stamped by sessiond, never by the client'. `partner_vh` (lines 73-86) has no `request_headers_to_remove` block and additionally sets `ExtAuthzPerRoute { disabled: true }`, then routes `/v1/` to the same `object_service` cluster. The backend derives the whole principal from those headers: `principalFrom` reads `X-Fleet-User`, `X-Fleet-Roles` and `X-Fleet-Tenant` off the request (service/auth.go:22-37), and `HasRole` returns true for any principal holding the literal role `admin` (line 41).
findings.impact: A request to `partners.example.com` carrying `X-Fleet-User: x`, `X-Fleet-Tenant: <victim>` and `X-Fleet-Roles: admin` is accepted as that tenant with universal authority — reading and overwriting any tenant's objects through `/v1/objects/`. The mTLS identity the comment relies on is never converted into the headers the backend actually reads, so disabling ext_authz removes the only thing that set them.
findings.recommendation: Add the same `request_headers_to_remove` list to `partner_vh` (and to every virtual host, or at the listener level so it cannot be forgotten), and map the partner's client-certificate identity into those headers explicitly — with a filter, not by trusting the client. Treat header-stripping as a listener-wide invariant rather than a per-virtual-host option.

triage.reason: The header strip is the control and it is scoped to one virtual host; the RBAC filter above only covers `/internal/` and `/admin/` paths, not `/v1/`, and ext_authz is explicitly disabled on this route.
The headers arrive on the client request and, with no removal rule, are forwarded verbatim to the upstream.
`typed_per_filter_config ... disabled: true` on a virtual host disables that filter for the whole host; there is no route in `partner_vh` that re-enables it.

findings.unaided_label: mesh: partner_vh disables ext_authz and does not strip x-fleet-* which auth.go trusts

findings.title: The object service publishes its port on the host, so every control in the Envoy edge can be walked around
findings.class: control bypassed by an alternative network path
findings.evidence: The `objects` service declares `ports: - "8081:8081"`, binding the container port to the host interface. Everything the edge enforces — the RBAC filter denying `/internal/` and `/admin/` from outside `10.20.0.0/16`, the ext_authz call to sessiond, and the `x-fleet-*` header strip — lives in the Envoy listener on 8080. A caller reaching `host:8081` speaks to the Go service directly, and the Go service performs no authentication of its own beyond reading the headers the edge was supposed to control. Note the contrast within the same file: `sessiond` publishes no ports and is reachable only on the mesh network.
findings.impact: Direct, unmediated access to the object service: forged `X-Fleet-*` identity on `/v1/objects/`, the unauthenticated `/admin` operator surface, and `/internal/diag` with its command injection. The entire security design of this service is 'the edge does it', and this line removes the edge.
findings.recommendation: Delete the host port mapping and let the service be reachable only on the `mesh` network, as `sessiond` already is. If direct access is needed for debugging, bind it to `127.0.0.1:8081:8081` and document it as a development-only override in a separate compose file.

triage.reason: A published port could be an intended bounded exposure, but nothing bounds it: the mapping has no interface prefix, so Docker binds 0.0.0.0, and the service behind it has no authentication of its own.
The compensating controls are all in envoy.yaml, and this path does not traverse Envoy.
This is the only compose file in scope and it carries the production-shaped configuration, including the mandatory `SESSION_SIGNING_KEY`.

findings.unaided_label: mesh: objects publishes 8081:8081, bypassing the Envoy edge entirely

findings.title: The operator and diagnostic handlers perform no authorization, unlike the object handler in the same mux
findings.evidence: `handleObject` calls `requireRole(w, r, "reader")` on GET and `requireRole(w, r, "writer")` on PUT (main.go:58, 76). The four handlers registered beside it — `/admin` (handleAdmin), `/internal/stats`, `/internal/diag`, `/internal/resolve` — call neither `requireRole` nor `principalFrom`; a `grep` for either symbol in admin.go and diag.go returns nothing. `handleAdmin` is the more consequential: a GET returns `store.Snapshot()`, the metadata of every object of every tenant (admin.go:47-55); `action: "usage"` lists objects for any `req.Tenant` the body names (line 41); `action: "restore"` writes arbitrary objects; `action: "purge-cache"` flushes the cache.
findings.impact: Anyone who reaches the service — via the published host port above, or via the `/admin` path the RBAC prefix does not cover — enumerates and rewrites every tenant's objects with no credential. The service's defence is entirely network-shaped, and both network assumptions are broken elsewhere in this same tree.
findings.recommendation: Call `requireRole(w, r, "admin")` at the top of `handleAdmin`, and gate the `/internal/*` handlers the same way. Application-layer authorization should be present regardless of the edge, since the edge is a separate artifact that can be misconfigured — as it is here.

triage.reason: The claimed compensating layer is the Envoy RBAC filter, and it is defeated two ways in this same tree: the published host port bypasses Envoy entirely, and the `/admin/` prefix does not match the `/admin` path the mux registers.
The second principal is another tenant: `Snapshot` and `usage` return objects across the `Tenant` field that `List` otherwise filters on.
Nothing declares the operator surface as intentionally open; the comment at admin.go:19 calls it 'the whole operator surface', which is an argument for gating it.

findings.unaided_label: mesh: /admin and /internal/* handlers never call requireRole

findings.title: The Envoy RBAC rule denies `/admin/` while the service registers `/admin`, so the operator path is not covered
findings.class: guard whose path does not match the route it protects
findings.evidence: The DENY policy's permissions are `url_path: { path: { prefix: "/internal/" } }` and `url_path: { path: { prefix: "/admin/" } }`, with the comment 'Operator surface: reachable only from the mesh subnet'. The Go mux registers `mux.HandleFunc("/admin", srv.handleAdmin)` (main.go:118) — a pattern without a trailing slash, which in `net/http.ServeMux` matches that exact path and nothing else. `/admin` does not carry the `/admin/` prefix, so the rule never matches the only URL the handler answers on, while `/admin/anything` matches the rule and 404s at the backend. `public_vh` routes prefix `/` to `object_service`, so `POST https://api.example.com/admin` reaches `handleAdmin`. The `/internal/` entry, by contrast, does match its routes (`/internal/stats`, `/internal/diag`, `/internal/resolve`) — the defect is in one of the two prefixes, which is why reading either file alone does not show it.
findings.impact: The operator surface the mesh-subnet restriction exists to protect is reachable from the public virtual host: a snapshot of every tenant's object metadata on GET, and `restore`/`purge-cache`/`usage` on POST, none of which the backend authorizes either.
findings.recommendation: Change the permission to `prefix: "/admin"` (or add an exact-path rule for `/admin`), and add a test that asserts a request to `/admin` from outside the subnet is denied. More durably: derive the deny list from the route table rather than restating it, so a path can never be registered without a matching rule.

triage.reason: The ext_authz filter runs on `public_vh`, but it resolves a session identity and returns identity headers; nothing in the configuration makes it deny an unauthenticated request to `/admin`, and the backend handler performs no authorization at all.

Envoy's `path.prefix` is a literal string prefix match; `/admin` does not start with `/admin/`, and Go's `ServeMux` treats a pattern without a trailing slash as an exact match. Both semantics are unambiguous.
Both the rule and the route registration are in the shipped artifacts, mounted read-only into the container at docker-compose.yml:8.

findings.unaided_label: mesh: RBAC denies prefix /admin/ but the mux serves exact path /admin

findings.title: The snapshot restore writer skips the tenant-ownership and quota checks its sibling enforces
findings.evidence: Two functions write an object. `Put` refuses to overwrite another tenant's key (`if existing, ok := s.meta[meta.Key]; ok && existing.Tenant != meta.Tenant { return errNotOwner }`, line 56) and enforces the quota (line 59), then recomputes `Size` and `Checksum` from the body it was given. `putRaw` calls `writeBlob` immediately and then credits `s.usage[meta.Tenant]` — no ownership check, no quota check, and `meta` (including `Tenant`, `Owner`, `Size` and `Checksum`) is taken from the caller verbatim. Its only caller is `restoreSnapshot`, which iterates `req.Objects` from the JSON request body (admin.go:60-61), so `ObjectMeta` is entirely request-controlled.
findings.impact: One POST to `/admin` with `action: "restore"` overwrites any object of any tenant, sets a false checksum on it (the value `handleObject` returns to readers as `X-Object-Checksum`), and writes past the tenant quota. Combined with the missing authorization on `/admin`, this is unauthenticated cross-tenant object replacement.
findings.recommendation: Have `restoreSnapshot` call `Put`, or move the ownership and quota invariants inside `writeBlob` so no writer can reach the disk around them. Recompute `Size` and `Checksum` from the body on every path rather than accepting them from the caller.

triage.reason: The invariants live in `Put`, and `putRaw` is a sibling that reaches the same `writeBlob` without them; `handleAdmin` adds no check of its own.
`adminEntry.Meta` is decoded straight from the request body (admin.go:14-17, 29), so `Tenant`, `Key` and `Checksum` are attacker-chosen.
The comment says the metadata 'comes from a previous export of this same store', but nothing establishes that provenance — the bytes arrive in an HTTP request body.

findings.unaided_label: mesh: putRaw skips the errNotOwner and quota checks that Put enforces

findings.title: The response cache is keyed on the URL path alone, so one tenant's objects and listings are served to another
findings.class: cross-tenant data exposure through a shared cache
findings.evidence: `key := r.URL.Path`, and the cache is consulted before `next.ServeHTTP` (lines 81-92), so a hit returns the stored body without the handler — and therefore without `requireRole` — ever running. The responses being cached are per-principal: `handleObject` returns `s.store.List(p.Tenant)` for the collection path and a tenant-checked body for an object path, where `p.Tenant` comes from the request headers, not from the URL. `withCache` wraps the whole mux (main.go:125), so `/admin` GET — the full cross-tenant metadata snapshot — is cached under that key too. Nothing sets `Vary`, and the stored header set is copied verbatim to the next caller.
findings.impact: Two defects in one line. Cross-tenant disclosure: tenant A reads `/v1/objects/report.pdf`, tenant B requests the same path within the 20-second TTL and receives A's bytes. And authorization bypass: an anonymous request to a cached path is served from memory before `requireRole` can reject it, since the hit branch returns first.
findings.recommendation: Include the identity in the key — `p.Tenant + "\x00" + r.URL.Path` — and resolve the principal before the cache lookup so an unauthenticated request can never be answered from it. Do not cache `/admin` or `/internal/*` at all; restrict `withCache` to the object routes rather than wrapping the mux.

triage.reason: `requireRole` is the control and the cache-hit branch returns before `next.ServeHTTP` is called, so the control is on the path that the hit skips.
The cached payloads are tenant object bodies and the cross-tenant metadata snapshot, not public content.
The boundary is the tenant: `Store.List` filters on `meta.Tenant` and `handleObject` compares `meta.Tenant != p.Tenant`, so the code treats a differing tenant as a second principal.

findings.unaided_label: mesh: withCache keys on r.URL.Path with no tenant, and serves hits before requireRole
